items.followUp: Name the three components of an ATP molecule.

rubric.why: Identifies the nitrogenous base and sugar in ATP.
rubric.description: Names adenine and ribose.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for both adenine and ribose.

rubric.why: Identifies the phosphate component of ATP.
rubric.description: Names the three phosphate groups.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that ATP has three phosphate groups.

modelAnswer: ATP consists of adenine, a ribose sugar and three phosphate groups.

items.followUp: Explain how an enzyme helps a substrate undergo a chemical reaction.

rubric.why: Shows how the enzyme interacts with its substrate.
rubric.description: The substrate binds to the enzyme, forming an enzyme-substrate complex.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for substrate binding or formation of the enzyme-substrate complex.

rubric.why: States how enzyme action makes the reaction easier.
rubric.description: The enzyme provides a pathway with lower activation energy.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the activation energy is lowered.

modelAnswer: The substrate binds to the enzyme's active site, forming an enzyme-substrate complex.
The enzyme provides an alternative reaction pathway with lower activation energy.

items.followUp: Who proposed the induced-fit model of enzyme action?

rubric.why: Identifies the scientist who proposed the model.
rubric.description: Names Emil Fischer.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for Emil Fischer.

rubric.why: Identifies when the model was proposed.
rubric.description: Gives the year 1894.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for 1894.

modelAnswer: Emil Fischer presented the lock-and-key model of enzyme action.
He presented it in 1894.

items.followUp: In which tissue are most red blood cells produced in adults?

rubric.why: Gives the adult site of red blood cell formation.
rubric.description: Red blood cells are formed in the red bone marrow of adults.
rubric.how: Award 2 marks for red bone marrow; award no mark for an incorrect site.

modelAnswer: In adults, red blood cells are formed in the red bone marrow.

items.followUp: Name two careers related to biology and state how each uses biological knowledge.

rubric.why: Identifies a biology-related career and its application.
rubric.description: Medicine: doctors use biology to diagnose and treat disease.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a suitable medical career with a relevant role.

rubric.why: Identifies a biology-related career and its application.
rubric.description: Agriculture: biological knowledge is used to improve crops and livestock.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for agriculture or farming with a relevant role.

rubric.why: Identifies a biology-related career and its application.
rubric.description: Forestry: biologists manage and conserve forests and their resources.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for forestry with a relevant role.

rubric.why: Identifies a biology-related career and its application.
rubric.description: Fisheries: biological knowledge is used to manage fish and other aquatic resources.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for fisheries with a relevant role.

modelAnswer: Medicine: doctors use biology to diagnose and treat diseases.
Agriculture: biological knowledge helps improve crops and livestock.
Forestry: biologists manage and conserve forests and their resources.
Fisheries: biological knowledge helps manage fish and other aquatic resources.

items.followUp: Name the three types of plastids and give one function of each.

rubric.why: Defines plastids and identifies where they occur.
rubric.description: Plastids are organelles found in plant cells and surrounded by a double membrane.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying plastids as plant-cell organelles (or giving the double membrane feature).

rubric.why: Identifies chloroplasts and their function.
rubric.description: Chloroplasts contain chlorophyll and carry out photosynthesis.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for chloroplasts and 1 mark for chlorophyll or photosynthesis.

rubric.why: Identifies chromoplasts and their pigment-related role.
rubric.description: Chromoplasts contain pigments that give colour to plant parts.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for chromoplasts and their role in colour or pigments.

rubric.why: Identifies leucoplasts and their storage role.
rubric.description: Leucoplasts are colourless plastids that store food.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for leucoplasts and food storage.

modelAnswer: Plastids are double-membraned organelles found in plant cells.
Chloroplasts contain chlorophyll and carry out photosynthesis.
Chromoplasts contain pigments that give colour to plant parts.
Leucoplasts are colourless plastids that store food.

items.followUp: Where do light reactions take place, and what are their main products?

rubric.why: Defines the light reactions by their dependence on light.
rubric.description: Light reactions are the light-dependent stage of photosynthesis.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying them as reactions that require light.

rubric.why: Describes the initial capture of light energy.
rubric.description: Chlorophyll absorbs light energy and its electrons become excited.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for chlorophyll absorbing light or exciting electrons.

rubric.why: Includes the splitting of water in the light reactions.
rubric.description: Water is split into hydrogen and oxygen (photolysis).
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that water is split.

rubric.why: Identifies oxygen as a product of water splitting.
rubric.description: Oxygen is released as a by-product.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for oxygen release.

rubric.why: Identifies the energy-rich products formed for the next stage of photosynthesis.
rubric.description: Light energy is used to form ATP and reduced NADP (NADPH).
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming both ATP and NADPH (reduced NADP).

modelAnswer: Light reactions are the light-dependent reactions of photosynthesis and take place in the thylakoid membranes of the chloroplasts.
Chlorophyll absorbs light energy, exciting its electrons.
Water molecules split by photolysis, providing hydrogen and releasing oxygen.
Oxygen is released as a by-product.
The absorbed energy is used to form ATP and reduced NADP (NADPH).

items.followUp: What is the difference between Rh-positive and Rh-negative blood?

rubric.why: States the basis of the ABO classification.
rubric.description: The ABO system is based on the presence or absence of A and B antigens on red blood cells.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the A and B red-cell antigens as the basis.

rubric.why: Names the four ABO blood groups.
rubric.description: The four ABO groups are A, B, AB and O.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming all four groups.

rubric.why: Shows understanding of the antibodies associated with ABO groups.
rubric.description: Plasma contains antibodies against the A or B antigens absent from that person's red blood cells.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly linking plasma antibodies to absent ABO antigens.

rubric.why: States the basis of the Rh classification.
rubric.description: The Rh system depends on whether the Rh antigen is present on red blood cells.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the Rh antigen on red blood cells.

rubric.why: Distinguishes Rh-positive from Rh-negative blood.
rubric.description: Rh-positive blood has the Rh antigen; Rh-negative blood lacks it.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly stating both conditions.

modelAnswer: The ABO system classifies blood according to the presence or absence of A and B antigens on red blood cells.
It has four groups: A, B, AB and O. Group A has A antigen, group B has B antigen, group AB has both, and group O has neither.
The plasma contains antibodies against the A or B antigens that are absent from a person's red blood cells.
The Rh system depends on the presence or absence of the Rh antigen on red blood cells.
A person with the Rh antigen is Rh-positive; a person without it is Rh-negative.
